scenes.headline: How a decision model points at its answer
scenes.sub: Kev: a Qwen3.5 base, a rank-16 LoRA and a pointer head.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Mallow! Kev makes a Qwen3.5 base pick from a list. Here's how it points, and what that costs.

scenes.label: The idea
scenes.text: Options are spans in one shared sequence, and a small head points at one. They can see each other, so their order matters.
scenes.say: Every option is a span in one shared sequence, and a small head points at one. The options can see each other, so their order matters.

steps.say: The question and every option go into one sequence. Each option ends in a closing tag, and a decide token comes last.
Qwen3.5 with a rank-sixteen LoRA reads it all. Its vocabulary head is dropped, because nothing is ever generated.
A small head projects each option's end state and the decide state to two hundred and fifty-six numbers, and takes a dot product: one score per option.

steps.note: 2 options or 16: no weight changes shape
steps.say: Send two options or sixteen, and no weight changes shape. The option set is just data.

scenes.title: Answers that flip when options are shuffled
scenes.say: The repository measured this two hundred and fifty-nine times. Shuffle the options, and fifteen point three percent of answers flip on the prototype. On a nine B base, one point eight.

scenes.title: The flip test, as a button
scenes.credit: jaredpalmer/kev playground, before the Qwen3.5 port

steps.say: The release's own playground shows it. A support message goes in, and each question gets a probability for every option it lists.
These buttons re-run one question under six option orders, and report whether the answer moved.

left.title: Option isolation
items: Each option its own branch, same positions
5.8 points lost at 4B; impossible on Qwen3.5
left.say: The fix: give every option its own branch. Nothing flips, but it cost five point eight points at four B, and Qwen3.5's recurrent layers can't do it.

right.title: Shared context, as shipped
right.say: So Kev ships the shared context, and the flips shrink with scale instead.

scenes.text: Order sensitivity is a dial, not a switch, and the dial is mostly capacity.
scenes.say: Order sensitivity is a dial, not a switch. And the dial is mostly capacity.

recap: Options are spans in one shared sequence
A bilinear head scores each against the decide state
Flips fall from 15.3% to 1.8% with scale
scenes.say: Options share one sequence, a small head points at one, and scale shrinks the flips.
